name: Janai Purnima at Gosaikunda
summary: On the full moon of Shrawan, thousands of Hindu pilgrims and shamans climb to Gosaikunda at 4,380 m to bathe in the lake Shiva is said to have made with his trident. It is the one night of the year when the lakeshore is crowded.
body: Janai Purnima is the day Brahmin and Chhetri men change the sacred thread (janai) they wear across the chest, and when everyone, of any caste, ties a yellow or red protective thread (doro) on the wrist. Across Nepal it is a household and temple festival. At Gosaikunda it becomes a mountain pilgrimage. Families walk up from Dhunche over two or three days, sleep in lodges, tents and stone shelters around the lake, and go down to the water at dawn on the full moon to bathe and offer flowers and coins at the Shiva shrine on the shore.

The lake draws pilgrims because of the story of the Samudra Manthan, the churning of the ocean. When Shiva drank the poison that rose from the churning, his throat burned, and he struck his trident into the mountain to bring out cold water. Gosaikunda is that water. Many pilgrims believe the lake is linked underground with the pond at the Kumbheshwar temple in Patan, so people who cannot make the climb bathe there on the same day.

The festival is also a gathering of dhami and jhankri, the shamans of the Tamang and other hill communities, who come in feathered headdresses with drums and bells and dance through the night around the lake. For a traveller this is the most striking part. Remember that this is worship, not a show, and that the trail is in monsoon: slippery, leech-ridden below 3,000 m and often in cloud. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Start from Dhunche at least three days before the full moon and plan a night at Laurebina to acclimatise.
Lodges around the lake fill completely; carry a sleeping bag rated to minus 5 °C even if you have a booking.
Ask before photographing shamans or people bathing, and keep flash off at night.

faqs.q: When is Janai Purnima at Gosaikunda?
faqs.a: It falls on the full moon of the Nepali month of Shrawan, which usually lands in August and occasionally late July. The exact date changes every year with the lunar calendar. Pilgrims arrive at the lake the evening before and bathe at dawn on the full-moon day. Check the official Nepali calendar and the current trail and road status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners join the Janai Purnima pilgrimage to Gosaikunda?
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign travellers walk the same trail from Dhunche with pilgrims, but they still need a Langtang National Park permit and, under the rule in force since April 2023, a licensed guide; check current status before you travel. Be respectful at the shore: bathing and offerings are religious acts, and the best places at the water belong to the people praying.

faqs.q: Is it safe to trek to Gosaikunda in August?
faqs.a: It is possible but harder than in autumn. August is monsoon: daily rain, cloud, leeches below about 3,000 m and landslide risk on the road to Dhunche. The lake area itself is cold, around 0 to 8 °C at night. Go with a guide who has done the festival walk before, allow a spare day, and check current road and trail status before you travel.

faqs.q: What do the shamans do at Gosaikunda during Janai Purnima?
faqs.a: Dhami and jhankri, the traditional healers of the Tamang and other hill communities, come to the lake to renew their power. They dance through the night in long white skirts and feather headdresses, beating drums and shaking bells, and many bathe in the lake at dawn. Some are accompanied by apprentices. Watch from a distance and ask before taking any photograph.

name: Sonam Lhosar
when: Second new moon after the winter solstice, Magh Shukla Pratipada (late January or February)
summary: Sonam Lhosar is the New Year of the Tamang and Hyolmo people, held on the first day of the bright half of Magh. In Rasuwa villages such as Gatlang and Briddim it means monastery visits, new clothes, Tamang Selo songs and the damphu drum.
body: Tamang and Hyolmo count years in a cycle of twelve animals, and Sonam Lhosar marks the turn from one animal year to the next. It falls on the second new moon after the winter solstice, which most years is Magh Shukla Pratipada in the Nepali calendar, so late January or February. Historically it came after the harvest was stored, when families had grain and time. In the days before, houses are cleaned and freshly plastered with mud, prayer flags are replaced and food is prepared in quantity.

On the day people visit the gompa and stupas, light butter lamps and receive blessings from the lama. Masked dances are performed at some monasteries to drive out harmful spirits. Then the village turns to music. Tamang Selo, the call-and-answer songs of the Tamang hills, is sung to the damphu, a round frame drum, and young people dance in lines in the courtyards. In Hyolmo and Rasuwa Tamang villages you will also see the syabru dance, with linked arms and stamping feet.

In Kathmandu, Sonam Lhosar is a public holiday and the open ground at Tundikhel fills with Tamang families in traditional dress. In Gatlang it is smaller and more personal: neighbours going from house to house with khata scarves, and plates of khapse fried biscuits and rice-flour babar. If you are staying in a Tamang homestay in this season, your hosts will include you; bring a small gift and accept the drink you are offered, even if you only touch it to your lips.
tips: Gatlang can be below freezing at night in February; homestays have blankets but bring a warm sleeping bag.
A white khata scarf and a small packet of sweets or fruit is a good gift for the household that hosts you.
Kathmandu's Tundikhel celebration is a good alternative if mountain roads are closed by snow or road works.

faqs.a: Sonam Lhosar falls on the second new moon after the winter solstice, usually Magh Shukla Pratipada in the Nepali calendar. That places it in late January or in February. The date moves each year with the lunar calendar, so check the official Nepali calendar for the year you travel, and check current status of mountain roads before you plan to be in a village for it.

It is the New Year of the Tamang and Hyolmo people, celebrated in Tamang areas around the Kathmandu Valley, in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, in Helambu, and in Sikkim and Darjeeling in India. It is different from Gyalpo Lhosar (the Sherpa and Tibetan New Year) and Tamu Lhosar (the Gurung New Year), which fall at other times of the year.

faqs.q: Can travellers attend Sonam Lhosar in Gatlang?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are staying in the village. There is no ticket and no stage: the festival happens at the gompa and in courtyards and homes. Staying in a community homestay is the natural way in. Your guide can introduce you, explain what is happening and tell you when it is fine to take photographs. Dress warmly and modestly.

faqs.q: What food is eaten at Sonam Lhosar?
faqs.a: Fried khapse biscuits, rice-flour flatbread called babar, and plenty of meat are typical, with local alcohol such as chhyang (fermented grain beer) and distilled rakshi. Hyolmo families also make thongsey. Homestay hosts usually cook a bigger meal than usual and share it with guests. Vegetarians should tell their host early; there will always be rice, dal and potatoes.

name: Sindure Jatra of Nuwakot
when: Spring, across Chaitra and Baisakh (April to early May)
summary: Nuwakot's spring festival for the goddess Bhairavi, also called Bhairavi Jatra. Wooden yosin poles go up at the goddess temples, the dhami priests lead processions to the Taleju temple, and everyone ends up red with sindur powder.
body: The Bhairavi temple stands about 200 m south of the seven-storey palace on the Nuwakot ridge. Its goddess, also called Gandaki Bhairavi after the Trishuli Gandaki river below, is the protector of the old fort town, and her festival is the biggest event of the Nuwakot year. Locals call it Sindure Jatra for the vermilion powder (sindur) that covers the crowd, and also Bhairavi Jatra. It runs over several weeks in spring, with the main days in April.

The festival is formally opened when a tall wooden pole, the yosin, is raised in front of the temples of Bhairavi and Budhi Bhairavi, and it closes when the pole is lowered again. In between come processions: the male and female dhami who serve the goddess, children representing Ganesh and Kumar, guthi members who fund and run the rituals, and musicians, all walking from the Bhairavi temple to the Taleju Bhawani temple on the hill and smearing each other with sindur on the way. The temple's dhami is a hereditary role; by custom he may not cross the Trishuli or Tadi rivers without the king's permission.

For a visitor, the best plan is to stay a night in Nuwakot during the main procession days, watch from the palace square and expect to be dusted with red. Dates follow the lunar calendar and local guthi decisions, so we confirm them each year with people in Nuwakot; check current status before you travel.
tips: Wear clothes you do not mind staining; sindur is hard to wash out of light cotton.
Put your camera in a zip bag between shots, as powder gets into lenses.
Stay overnight in Nuwakot rather than driving back the same day, so you catch the morning rituals.

faqs.q: When is Sindure Jatra in Nuwakot?
faqs.a: It is a spring festival in the Nepali months of Chaitra and Baisakh. In 2024 it began in early April, the yosin pole was raised on 22 April and the festival closed in early May. Dates move with the lunar calendar and are fixed locally each year, so check current status before you travel and ask us to confirm the main procession days.

faqs.q: What is the yosin pole at Nuwakot's festival?
faqs.a: The yosin is a tall wooden pole raised in front of the Bhairavi and Budhi Bhairavi temples. Its raising marks the official start of the festival and its lowering marks the end. Pole-raising is an old feature of Newar festivals in the Kathmandu Valley as well, for example at Bhaktapur's Bisket Jatra, and reflects the Newar roots of Nuwakot's temple town.

faqs.q: Can tourists take part in Sindure Jatra?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a public festival in the streets and temple squares, and visitors are welcome to watch the processions and will likely be dabbed with sindur. Do not enter the inner shrine of the Bhairavi temple, follow your guide's lead about where to stand, and ask before photographing the dhami during rituals.

faqs.q: How do we get to Nuwakot for the festival?
faqs.a: Nuwakot is about 75 km from Kathmandu by road via Kakani and Bidur, normally 3 to 3.5 hours by private car. Bidur and the Trishuli valley floor were damaged by the flood of 26 August 2026, so road works may add time; check current status before you travel. We suggest one or two nights at The Famous Farm or a local guesthouse on the ridge.
